section.title: Chapter review and discovery problems
section.p: This chapter began with a practical problem:
section.md: \text{Applications give us integrals. How do we evaluate them?}
section.p: The answer was not one method. It was a collection of ways to recognize structure.

Substitution reverses the chain rule. Integration by parts reverses the product rule. Trigonometric identities reshape trigonometric expressions. Trigonometric substitution uses right triangles to simplify square roots. Partial fractions split rational functions into simpler pieces. Improper integrals add one more demand: before evaluating, we must ask whether the accumulated amount is finite.
So the main lesson is not a list of tricks. It is a habit:
section.md: \text{Read the integrand before choosing a method.}

subsection.title: The chapter in one map
subsection.p: A good integration method answers a specific question about the integrand.

table.title: Structure, guiding questions, and integration methods

row.cell: An inside function and its derivative
Is the chain rule hiding here?
A product where one factor simplifies when differentiated
Did the product rule create this?
Powers of \sin x, \cos x, \tan x, or \sec x
Can I save a differential and rewrite the rest?
Which Pythagorean identity matches the square root?
Is the rational function proper, and how does the denominator factor?
An infinite interval or an infinite discontinuity
Does the limiting accumulated amount exist?

subsection.p: The same integral may yield to more than one method. The goal is not to find the only path. The goal is to find a path that makes the structure visible.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: Exact integration is powerful, but it is not the whole story.
Some integrals have elementary antiderivatives:
Some have antiderivatives that require special functions:

Some come from data instead of formulas. A speedometer may give readings every second. A thermometer may give temperatures every hour. A sensor may give force measurements at discrete positions. In those cases, there may be no formula to antidifferentiate.
But the accumulated amount may still be exactly what we need.
is a real number. The length
is a real length. The work computed from measured force data is real work.
So the next question is not
subsection.md: \text{Can we always find an exact antiderivative?}
subsection.p: The answer is no.
The better question is
subsection.md: \text{How can we approximate an integral, and how can we know how accurate the approximation is?}
subsection.p: That question leads to numerical integration, error estimates, and computation.
